text: In the lesson on retrieval, we searched by meaning: embed the question, then fetch the passages whose vectors point the same way. Now imagine a support assistant asked about error code E1047. The embedding of that code carries almost no meaning, because the model has rarely seen it, yet it is precisely the thing a matching document must contain. Search engines solved this kind of exact matching long before embeddings existed, and their answer still sits underneath most search systems today. It is called BM25.

The first idea is the inverted index, which works like the index at the back of a textbook. Instead of reading every page to find a word, you look the word up and get the list of pages that mention it. A search index stores, for every word, a postings list: the documents that contain it and how many times. A query then touches only the postings of its own words, which is why keyword search stays fast over millions of documents.

Next, the index has to score each document it finds. A page that mentions refund five times is probably more about refunds than a page that mentions it once, but it is not five times more relevant. BM25 lets the contribution of repeated words saturate, rising quickly at first and then flattening out, much as the first few witnesses make a case and the twentieth adds very little. A parameter called k one sets how soon that flattening begins.

Not every word is equally informative either. The word the appears in nearly every document, so finding it tells you nothing, while a rare code that appears in three documents out of a million is strong evidence. Inverse document frequency, or IDF, turns this into a weight: it is the logarithm of how surprising it is to find the word at all, so rare words count heavily and common words count for almost nothing.

There is one more bias to correct. A very long document contains more words simply by being long, so it would match almost any query a little. BM25 compares each document's length with the average and scales the word counts down for long documents. A second parameter, b, sets how strongly: at zero length is ignored, and at one the correction is complete. Values near k one of one point two and b of three quarters are common starting points.

Put the pieces together and the score of a document is a sum over the query's words, where each word contributes its rarity weight multiplied by its saturated, length corrected count. For the query refund E1047, the common word refund adds a little to many documents, while the rare code adds a great deal to the few that contain it, so the document about that exact error rises to the top.

The weakness is the mirror image of its strength. BM25 matches surface forms, so a question about getting money back will not find a page that only says refund. Embeddings handle exactly that case well, and they stumble on exactly the codes and names that BM25 handles well. The natural next step is to run both and combine their results, which is the subject of the next lesson, hybrid search.
